You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- What the failing test checks:
  - VarianceTest.testEvaluateArraySegmentWeighted copies the first 5 values/weights from testArray/testWeightsArray into new arrays of length 5 (arrayZero/weightZero).
  - It then asserts that the weighted variance computed over the whole 5-element arrays equals the weighted variance computed over the segment [0, 5) of the original arrays.

- Call flow in the code:
  - stat.evaluate(testArray, testWeightsArray, 0, 5) resolves to Variance.evaluate(double[], double[], int, int).
    - This method computes the weighted mean correctly for the segment using Mean.evaluate(values, weights, begin, length) (lines 323–325 in Variance).
    - It then calls Variance.evaluate(values, weights, mean, begin, length) (lines 324–325).
  - stat.evaluate(arrayZero, weightZero) resolves to the overload that computes weighted variance over the entire provided arrays (which are length 5), so its internal total-weight summation covers exactly those 5 weights.

- The defect:
  - In Variance.evaluate(double[] values, double[] weights, double mean, int begin, int length), the accumulators for the numerator are correctly computed over the segment [begin, begin + length) (lines 513–517).
  - However, the total weight sum (sumWts) is incorrectly computed over the entire weights array (0 to weights.length) instead of just the segment (lines 519–522):
    - for (int i = 0; i < weights.length; i++) { sumWts += weights[i]; }
  - This violates the segment restriction and mismatches the numerator computed on the segment. It also affects the bias-correction denominator (sumWts - 1.0) or the uncorrected denominator (sumWts) (lines 524–528).
  - By contrast, Mean.evaluate(double[], double[], int, int) correctly uses the segment for summing weights via Sum.evaluate(weights, begin, length) (line 209 in Mean), which is why the mean calculation is correct.

- Why the test fails:
  - For the first branch (stat.evaluate(arrayZero, weightZero)), sumWts equals the sum of the 5 selected weights because the arrays themselves are length 5.
  - For the second branch (stat.evaluate(testArray, testWeightsArray, 0, 5)), sumWts incorrectly includes all weights in testWeightsArray, not just the first 5, leading to a different denominator. This causes the two computed variances to differ, breaking the equality assertion.

- Conclusion:
  - The bug is that Variance.evaluate(double[], double[], double, int, int) ignores the begin/length window when summing weights for the denominator and bias correction, effectively “grabbing the whole dataset,” exactly as described in the bug report. The fix is to compute sumWts over the specified segment [begin, begin + length), mirroring how Mean handles segmented weights.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
